title: Where did this evidence come from?
outcome: You can name the process that produced a piece of evidence, then pick the one test that could prove a conclusion wrong.
subject: critical-thinking

concepts.title: Where did this evidence come from?
concepts.centralCause: The way evidence was collected (what was picked, what could be seen, who passed it on) shapes what it can show. So first name that process, then look for the one check the conclusion could fail. This applies when you know, or can ask, how the evidence got to you.
conditions: You can say how the evidence was gathered or passed on
The set of possibilities is known (as in the card puzzle)
A test is only useful if one of its possible results could contradict the conclusion
Shared origin means dependence, not falsehood

cards.title: Test where the rule can break

fact.statement: To check a rule, turn over only the cards that could show it false. A result that fits the rule but could never break it proves little.
conditions: The rule is 'a triangle has a blue back'
Only four cards exist: triangle, circle, blue, orange
Only shapes and colours named exist
fact.source: Author's own notes for a critical-thinking micro-course (16-18); all numbers are teaching numbers, not measurements. hook.question: Four cards lie on the table. You may turn over only two to check a rule. Why is the blue card a waste?
hook.predictPrompt: Rule: a triangle has a blue back. Cards: triangle, circle, blue, orange. Which two do you turn, and why?

cards.explanation: A rule fails only when it is broken. This rule breaks if a triangle has a non-blue back. So turn the triangle. Turn the orange card too, because a triangle behind it would break the rule. Blue is useless: a triangle on blue fits the rule, and a circle on blue breaks nothing.

action.instruction: Thought experiment: now orange becomes blue. Predict which cards you need, then compare with the first set.
constants: Only these shapes and colours exist

question.prompt: A warehouse rule says fragile parcels are reinforced. You have records of: fragile, not fragile, reinforced, not reinforced. Which two do you open, and why?

key.expectedCause: Open the fragile parcel and the not-reinforced parcel, because only those could break the rule (a fragile parcel that is not reinforced). Opening the reinforced or not-fragile ones cannot contradict the rule.
acceptable: Says: look for a fragile one without reinforcement from both sides
Says: reinforced and not-fragile cannot show a violation
key.typicalMistake: Picking the reinforced parcel to find confirming examples, which cannot break the rule.
key.followUp: What could you find inside the reinforced parcel that would break the rule?

criteria.example: Open fragile and not reinforced. A fragile parcel without reinforcement would break the rule; a reinforced parcel can't.

fact.statement: A correct answer may come through a different channel than the one you assume. Remove or change one possible channel and see whether the answer changes.

question.prompt: A bot labels pictures as wolf on snow and dog on grass. You swap only the background of one picture. If the label changes, what does that show, and what if it does not change?

fact.statement: If you only see what survived or returned, the evidence misses what stopped things from coming back. A lightly marked part may be vulnerable or rarely hit.

cards.title: A flag is not a verdict

fact.statement: When the target group is small, false alarms from the large non-target group can outnumber true hits. Changing how common the target is changes how much a flag means.
conditions: Model: 1 in 1,000 has a condition, all tested, every real case is detected, 5 percent of the rest are wrongly flagged
Same group and test when the condition becomes 1 of 2
fact.source: Author's own notes for a critical-thinking micro-course (16-18); all numbers are teaching numbers, not measurements. Classic tasks attributed, no participant results used: Wason selection task (described 1968); Pfungst, Clever Hans (1911); Wald, aircraft damage memoranda (1943, CNA reprint 1980); the test problem is a teaching model (task attributed to Casscells et al., 1978); the 1835 Moon Hoax per Library of Congress. Adult reference only, no text copied: OpenStax Introductory Statistics 2e 1.2 and 3.5, Introduction to Philosophy 2.2 (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) — https://www.cna.org/reports/1980/0204320000.pdf

hook.question: A test catches every real case. Why can most of its flags still be wrong?
hook.predictPrompt: In 1,000 people, 1 has the condition and 5 percent of the rest are wrongly flagged. Roughly how many flags are real, and why?

cards.explanation: In this model, the one real case is flagged. About 5 percent of the other 999 are also flagged, roughly 50 people. So about 1 real flag stands against about 50 false. The big non-target group produces many false alarms. This is a model, not a medical conclusion.

action.instruction: Thought experiment: now the condition is in 1 of 2 people, same group and same test. Predict the share of real flags, then compare. It is about 95 percent real.
action.changedCondition: How common the condition is: 1 in 1,000 versus 1 in 2

key.typicalMistake: Saying a flagged file is almost surely damaged because the checker finds all damaged ones.

cards.title: Three sources or one echo

fact.statement: Several sources that copy one origin add no new observation. Shared source means dependence, not that the claim is false.
conditions: The reprints do not make their own check
They trace back to one source

hook.question: Three outlets say the same thing. Why might that still be only one piece of evidence?
hook.predictPrompt: Three AI assistants cite one press release about a battery. How many independent pieces of evidence do you have, and why?

cards.explanation: In 1835 the New York Sun printed a story that others reprinted. Reprints without their own check add no observation. If sources share one origin, they depend on it. That does not make the claim false. It means you should check the origin, not count the copies.

question.prompt: Three AI assistants all cite one press release saying a new battery lasts twice as long. How strong is this as three-way support, and what would you do next?

key.expectedCause: They share one source, so it is one piece of evidence repeated, not three independent checks. This does not prove the claim false. Next, look for the original data or an independent test.
acceptable: Suggests checking the press release's evidence or an independent source
key.typicalMistake: Saying three agreeing assistants make it three times more certain, or that a shared source proves it false.
key.followUp: Does a shared source mean the claim is wrong?

criteria.example: All three rest on one press release, so it is one source echoed. That doesn't make it false, but I'd look for an independent test.
